name: “Treatment only works if someone really wants it.”

blocks.content: No one should be forced into treatment they don’t consent to
And it’s true that lasting change isn’t likely until a person is genuinely prepared. That said, Change is often gradual — and support along the way matters.
message_bubble
Fact: Readiness can be supported and built.
Even when someone isn’t ready to stop drinking completely, we can still help create safer conditions, strengthen supports, and reduce pressure by:

items: Providing clear, non-judgmental information about options.
Helping address underlying stressors — like burnout, anxiety, or isolation.
Build alternative coping strategies so alcohol isn’t the only relief.

name: “Medication is just replacing one thing with another”

blocks.content: Medication is not a silver bullet.
It is meant to complement counselling, lifestyle changes, and social supports as one part of a broader care plan.
doctors
Fact: Medications are tools, not substitutes.

Evidence-based medications for alcohol use disorder do not create a new addiction or intoxication, and are typically only taken temporarily. They work by reducing cravings, decreasing the rewarding effects of alcohol, or helping prevent heavy drinking episodes. They are intended as practical support that can make other changes more achievable by:

items: Clearing mental space to focus on therapy and skill-building.
Giving the brain and body time to heal.
Helping people feel more stable and in control.

blocks.content: This belief comes from an outdated “all-or-nothing” view of recovery.
It assumes that any return to drinking cancels out prior effort — and that success means never struggling again.
x_marks_the_spot
Fact: Recovery is often non-linear.
A return to drinking after a period of change does not erase progress. Many chronic health conditions involve flare-ups or setbacks, and alcohol use disorder is no different.

Relapse can signal unmet needs, new stressors, or gaps in support — not a lack of character or commitment. It can also reflect the reality that change is hard and humans are imperfect. With the right response, a setback can become information: an opportunity to adjust the care plan, strengthen coping strategies, and build more durable supports.
Progress still counts. Healing is measured over time, not by a single moment.
It would be convenient if change alone fixed everything overnight
Physically, emotionally, and relationally. In reality, it’s rarely that simple.
hourglass
Fact: Healing takes time, and often requires broader change.

While the body begins to recover soon after alcohol use decreases, full healing can take weeks, months, or longer, depending on the person and their history. Recovery also often involves practical life adjustments: new routines, boundaries, friendships, or even changes in work or environment. Relationships may need rebuilding. Coping strategies must be practiced and maintained. The person may grow and shift in the process. It’s part of building a life that supports long-term stability.

name: “You have to hit rock bottom before I can help you.”

blocks.content: Hitting rock bottom does not help most people change their ways.
Harshness does not jolt people into changing.
low_battery
Fact: Hitting rock bottom can be more destructive than helpful.

When we are supporting people who are using substances, it is important to focus on building relationships based on safety and trust. If people do not find connection in their lives with other people, they will find something to connect to – including substances. If we leave people on their own in order for them to ‘hit rock bottom’, we lose these opportunities to connect and provide support.

name: “If you really loved me, you would stop using.”

blocks.content: People experiencing addiction do care for their loved ones
And deeply understand that their substance use causes their family, friends, and community pain and guilt.
helping_hand
Fact: Addiction is not a choice.
Ending addiction is much more complicated than “just saying no”. One of the most important things we can do is support the people we care about along their healing journey
Have open conversations and talk about substance use.
Learn more about addiction and harm reduction.
